summary: The bill creates a new National Institute for Biomedical Research and Development within NIH that conducts or funds full-cycle R&D on drugs, devices, and biologics, owns resulting patents and data, prioritizes public-health needs via a governing board, and makes products available through public manufacturing at cost or nonexclusive licensing with cost-plus terms.

scores.thoughts: The bill authorizes $90 billion in appropriations for FY2027 to establish and operate a new National Institute for Biomedical Research and Development within NIH. It also permits construction of facilities, hiring of personnel, contracting, and acquisition activities. This directly and substantially expands federal outlays on biomedical R&D and related infrastructure.
The bill contains no provisions altering tax rates, credits, deductions, or revenue measures of any kind.

The legislation creates a federal institute to conduct full-cycle public development of drugs, devices, and biologics, own resulting patents, license them on public-interest terms (including cost-plus or free to nonprofits), and ensure equitable pricing and supply. This constitutes a significant expansion of direct public-sector involvement in pharmaceutical production and pricing, moving away from a purely private/market-driven model.
No provisions address firearms, background checks, or gun regulations.
No provisions address immigration, visas, border policy, or related protections.
No provisions address reproductive health services, abortion access, or funding restrictions.
The bill references existing DoD facilities only as potential sources of technology to monitor; it neither authorizes nor alters military or defense spending.
No provisions address environmental regulation, emissions, or climate policy.
No provisions alter eligibility, funding, or administration of welfare, SNAP, Medicaid, or similar programs.
No provisions address schools, student aid, or education policy.
The bill concerns development and pricing of approved medicines and medical products; it does not address criminal penalties, decriminalization, or enforcement related to controlled substances.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, incarceration, or criminal procedure.
While the bill references technology transfer and access in low- and middle-income countries, it does not modify tariffs, trade agreements, or trade enforcement mechanisms.
The bill authorizes $90 billion in new mandatory-style spending without any offsetting revenue or cuts, thereby increasing the deficit and national debt trajectory.
No provisions address nondiscrimination protections, gender identity, or LGBTQ+ legal rights.
The bill facilitates global access to medicines developed by the institute but does not authorize or modify foreign assistance programs or appropriations.
No provisions address voting access, election administration, or campaign finance.
The bill mandates open sharing of clinical and preclinical data generated by the institute but does not impose new regulatory oversight on private technology companies or alter privacy statutes.
No provisions address collective bargaining, union rights, or labor standards.
No provisions address religious exemptions, conscience protections, or conflicts between civil rights and religious liberty.
